title: New-to-The-World and New-to-Self: Academic Research Funding and Impact

summary.oneLiner: Research funders appear to over-reward track records of scientists pursuing new-to-the-world work and undervalue those exploring fields new to themselves, misaligning grants with impact.
summary.overview: Because research outcomes are hard to predict, funders lean on scientists' past records when deciding who gets money. This working paper argues that how much a track record counts depends on the kind of exploration a scientist is doing. Evaluators who are not close to the research frontier may give too much weight to the records of scientists doing "new-to-the-world" work (novel to science) and too little to those doing "new-to-self" work (novel only to the researcher). The authors predict, and report that their data support, a mismatch between the funding scientists receive and their later publications and impact.
summary.question: How do a scientist's track record and the type of exploration they pursue jointly shape the funding they receive, and does that funding line up with their subsequent research performance?
summary.method: Comparison of funding and subsequent publication output and impact across a matched sample of scientists pursuing different kinds of exploration. Estimation details are not stated in the available sources.
summary.data: A matched sample of 26,253 academic scientists at a large Midwestern US university, 1970 to 2005.
findings: Funding amounts reflect both a scientist's track record and the type of exploration they pursue.
Evaluators appear to overweight the track records of scientists doing new-to-the-world research.
Evaluators appear to undervalue the track records of scientists doing new-to-self research.
The result is a mismatch between the grants scientists receive and their later research output and impact, as the authors predicted.
summary.whyItMatters: The paper speaks to how organizations hand out money for uncertain projects: if evaluators read track records differently depending on the type of exploration, funding may drift away from researchers whose work later has more impact. It is a working paper (listed as to be resubmitted on Nandkumar's CV).
